title: Passover: it would have been enough
hookLine: a song counting gifts one by one
tomorrow: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)

cards: Partway through the seder, after a long stretch of reading, the energy changes.
Someone starts a song with a three-syllable chorus, and suddenly everyone, the uncle checking his phone, the toddler under the table, is shouting it. Day, day, enu. Day, day, enu.
In some Persian and Afghan Jewish families, people grab scallions and playfully swat each other during the chorus, recalling the whips of slavery. It can get rowdy.
And underneath the noise, the song is doing something careful: counting.

teach.b: Dayenu means it would have been enough for us. The song walks through the Exodus in fifteen steps, each one a gift. If God had brought us out of Egypt, and not brought judgment on the Egyptians: dayenu.
If God had split the sea, and not led us through on dry ground: dayenu. If God had fed us manna, and not given us Shabbat. If God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah.
All the way to the land of Israel and the Temple.

teach.h: IF ONLY THIS, IT WOULD BE ENOUGH.
teach.b: Fifteen times the table shouts: that would have been enough. The Haggadah introduces it with a line: how many good steps God has done for us.

The full song appears in an early prayer order compiled in Babylonia by a scholar named Amram Gaon. Some lines sound strange taken literally. Would standing at Sinai without the Torah really have been enough?
Teachers have answered in different ways. One answer: the song isn't making a claim about history. It's training the eye.
Each step deserved a whole thank-you of its own, so don't let the gifts blur into one lump.

teach.h: HOW MUCH MORE, FOR ALL OF THEM.
teach.b: Then the Haggadah turns it around: how much more should we be grateful, since God did all of them.
It's easy to give thanks in bulk. Dayenu gives thanks one gift at a time.

how: At the seder, after the telling of the plagues, families sing Dayenu together, with everyone joining the chorus; in some Persian and Afghan Jewish homes, people playfully tap each other with scallions during the song.

o: it would have been enough for us
we have waited long enough for this
the day of our going out of Egypt

p: it would have been enough for us
the number of steps in the song

s: it's in the Haggadah; its full text appears in Amram Gaon's prayer order.
the song counts fifteen gifts, one at a time
from leaving Egypt to the Temple.
after the fifteen, the Haggadah adds a paragraph about all of them together
how much more grateful we should be, since God did them all.

games.q: you're singing Dayenu. the next line: if God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah. what does the table shout?
o: dayenu: it would have been enough.
nothing: the song skips that line.
games.why: dayenu. even standing at the mountain, the song says, was a gift worth its own thank-you.

practice: Think of one good thing in your life, maybe a person, and break it into steps: if they had only shown up once, enough; if they had only stayed, enough.
Go slowly, one gift at a time, saying dayenu after each, out loud or in your head.

wordCard.voice: Dayenu. It would have been enough for us: the seder's song of fifteen gifts, counted one by one. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: enough for us, from dai, enough.

carryVoice: Your line: it would have been enough. Fifteen gifts, each one counted on its own. Until tomorrow.
